nameStory: The Fork-tailed Flycatcher gets its name from its spectacular deeply forked tail, which looks like a giant dinner fork when spread wide. Males sport especially long, dramatic tail feathers that can be nearly as long as their body, making them unmistakable when they flash that signature silhouette against the sky.
description: The Fork-tailed Flycatcher is a striking medium-sized bird with the most dramatic tail of any flycatcher you'll see in New England. These elegant birds have gray and white plumage with black caps, but it's that incredibly long, deeply forked tail that stops people in their tracks. They're part of the kingbird family and share that group's bold, upright posture and habit of perching prominently while hunting insects. At roughly robin-sized, they're built for agile aerial maneuvers.

idTips.label: Forked Tail
idTips.description: Extremely long, deeply forked black tail that streams behind like ribbons when flying - males have especially dramatic tail streamers that flutter distinctively in flight

idTips.label: Black Cap
idTips.description: Solid black crown and back of head contrasting sharply with white throat and gray body - looks like they're wearing a sleek black helmet

idTips.label: Perching Behavior
idTips.description: Sits conspicuously on fence posts, utility wires, or exposed branches with upright, alert posture - tail often held slightly spread to show the fork

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Graceful, buoyant flight with those long tail streamers trailing behind - often hovers briefly before diving after insects

idTips.label: Body Colors
idTips.description: Clean gray back and wings with bright white underparts - the contrast is crisp and well-defined, never muddy or mottled

habitat: Fork-tailed Flycatchers are extremely rare visitors to New England, typically showing up in open areas like coastal grasslands, farm fields, and meadows with scattered perches. When they do appear, look for them in agricultural areas or coastal plains where they can find the open hunting grounds and prominent perches they prefer.

seasonality.spring: Very rarely seen during spring migration, usually May through early June. Any sighting would be exceptional and worth reporting to birding networks.
seasonality.summer: Occasional summer visitors, though still extremely rare. Most likely to be seen perching conspicuously in open areas during warm weather when insects are active.
seasonality.fall: Peak time for vagrant sightings in New England, typically September through October when southern populations are migrating and some individuals wander far off course.
seasonality.winter: Virtually never seen in winter as these birds cannot survive New England's cold temperatures and lack of flying insects.

funFact: Fork-tailed Flycatchers are such notorious wanderers that they've been spotted as far north as Canada despite their normal range extending from Mexico to Argentina - they're like the ultimate avian road-trippers, sometimes ending up thousands of miles from where they belong!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Scissor-tailed Flycatcher, but Fork-tailed has a much blacker head and grayer body, while Scissor-tailed shows peachy-pink sides and a lighter gray head. Remember: Fork-tailed = blacker head and grayer body, Scissor-tailed = peachy sides and lighter overall.
contextualKnowledge: Fork-tailed Flycatchers are considered vagrant birds in New England - meaning they're far outside their normal range when seen here. With only 36 recorded observations, spotting one would be the birding equivalent of finding a four-leaf clover, making every sighting a notable event worth documenting.
compareHints: Unlike its kingbird relatives, the Fork-tailed Flycatcher has that unmistakable extremely long, forked tail that no other kingbird possesses. Eastern Kingbirds have white tail bands and shorter, squared tails, while other kingbirds lack the dramatic tail streamers entirely. The Fork-tailed's combination of black cap, gray back, and ribbon-like tail makes it impossible to mistake for any other kingbird species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eastern Kingbirds are the only kingbird species that regularly breeds in New England, making identification easier than in western regions where multiple kingbird species overlap.
Western Kingbirds are easily distinguished from their Eastern Kingbird cousins by their bright yellow underparts versus the Eastern's clean white belly.

Among its kingbird relatives, the Scissor-tailed Flycatcher is instantly distinguished by its extraordinarily long, forked tail - Eastern Kingbirds have much shorter, square tails with white tips, while Western Kingbirds have moderately long tails but nothing approaching the dramatic streamers of the Scissor-tailed.
Among the kingbirds, Tropical Kingbird's bright yellow belly immediately separates it from the white-bellied Eastern Kingbird.
Unlike Eastern Kingbirds with their stark black caps and white tail bands, Gray Kingbirds are much more subtly colored in pale gray and white.
Unlike the familiar Eastern Kingbird with its clean white underparts and white-tipped tail, Cassin's Kingbird shows the distinctive white throat against gray chest pattern.
